items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I did that with Glenn Osser [born Abe Osser]... I did it for 22 years with him.

ctx.x: That started in the ’60s. I did that with Glenn Osser [born Abe Osser]. It’s odd, because when he asked me to do it, I wasn’t being hired to play jazz or anything. They had a lot of girls that used to come down. They’d sing the arias, the operatic arias, and most of the players that they had there were the fellows who had been doing club dates. They were good players, but they never had any experience playing these things. So Abe hired me just to play those things. It’s sort of a twist, but it was really nice. I…
What was that like, to play for the . . . ?

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: Like when we did the Miss America pageant it was always a joy because he wrote such beautiful arrangements.

ctx.x: Was there certain arrangers whose names that you liked to see on the chart, and certain that you didn’t?

Oh yeah. Neal Hefti was one of them. Neal Hefti, now because you asked me that I can’t think of some, but there were several guys who you just broke your neck getting to the studio to work for them because it was always, always a joy. Billy Byers, guys like that, Kent Hopkins. These guys could write and Buddy Weed was another one, Glenn Osser, who was the conductor of the Miss America pageant. Like when we did the Miss America pageant it was always a joy because he wrote such beautiful arrangements. Everything…
What do you think of the state of music these days? How’s that for an open question?

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: And Abe Osser was standing and looking, he couldn’t believe that this was happening, with a straight face.

ctx.x: And his trumpet solo? Can you tell me how that happened?

We were doing “Juke Box Saturday Night.” It was a series they had on channel 13. And when the trumpet solo came on, Johnny Frosk stood up and played “In the Mood” or something. The solo he played was note for note from some other piece. It had nothing to do with this harmonically or otherwise. And he just played it. And Abe Osser was standing and looking, he couldn’t believe that this was happening, with a straight face. It was unbelievable.
Was it “String of Pearls” or something?
